  <div class="eyebrow page-eyebrow">Customer Analytics · Case Study</div>
  <h1 class="page-title">Phantom churners</h1>
  <p class="article-deck">
    My churn model scored an AUC of 0.79 and ranked customers beautifully. It also
    predicted that <em>12,180</em> of 30,000 subscribers were about to leave, in a market where the
    real number was closer to 700. Both things were true at once — and only one of them mattered for
    the budget.
  </p>

  <dl class="article-meta">
    <div><dt>Role</dt><dd>Analyst</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Case</dt><dd>Telecom churn &amp; retention economics</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Stack</dt><dd>Python · polars · pyrsm · XGBoost</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Course</dt><dd>MGTA 455, Rady School of Management</dd></div>
  </dl>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The assignment</h2>
    <p>A Singapore mobile carrier wanted to know which retention programs to fund. The chain of
    reasoning is standard: predict who will churn, work out which interventions move that number,
    convert the movement into lifetime value, and set a budget from there.</p>
    <p>Every step after the first depends on the model producing a <strong>probability</strong>, not
    just a ranking. That distinction is the whole story here.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Picking a model</h2>
    <p>I compared logistic regression against two tree ensembles on a 39,000-row training sample,
    using log transforms on the skewed spend and usage variables:</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
    <table class="article-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Model</th><th>AUC</th><th>Note</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Logistic regression</td><td>≈0.70</td><td>Baseline, transformed features</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Random forest</td><td>0.713</td><td>Untuned</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Random forest (tuned)</td><td>0.727</td><td></td></tr>
        <tr class="dim"><td>XGBoost</td><td>0.888</td><td>Training AUC — overfit</td></tr>
        <tr><td>XGBoost (tuned)</td><td>0.793</td><td>Selected</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Tuned XGBoost won on test AUC and held its shape between train and test on the gains curves.
    A defensible choice, and by every metric I had been taught to check, a finished model.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Then I looked at the level</h2>
    <p>Applying that model to the 30,000-customer representative sample — the one built to mirror the
    actual subscriber base — produced a mean predicted churn probability of <strong>40.6%</strong>.
    The real market rate is about 2%.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-stats">
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">0.793</div><div class="article-stat-l">Test AUC — genuinely good ranking</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">40.6%</div><div class="article-stat-l">Mean predicted churn</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">~2%</div><div class="article-stat-l">Actual market churn</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">17×</div><div class="article-stat-l">Overstatement of churners</div></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>The cause was in the training data. The 39,000-row sample had been built at roughly
    <strong>50% churn</strong> — deliberately oversampled so the models would have enough positive
    cases to learn from. That is a sensible thing to do for estimation, and a catastrophic thing to
    forget afterwards. The model learned the shape of churn risk on a world where half of everyone
    leaves, then reported those probabilities into a world where one in fifty does.</p>
    <p>The fix was to re-estimate on the full million-row dataset, which carries the true ~2% base
    rate — same features, same hyperparameters, no retuning. About 682,000 training rows.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Mean predicted churn on the 30,000-customer representative sample</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">Identical model specification. The only change is the base rate of the
        data it was fitted on.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-chart-scroll"><svg id="chart1" class="article-chart-sm" viewBox="0 0 700 300" role="img"
        aria-label="Bar chart comparing mean predicted churn of 40.6 percent from the oversampled model versus 2.38 percent from the full-data model, against a 2 percent market rate"></svg></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tip1"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
      <table class="article-table">
        <thead><tr><th>Trained on</th><th>Churn in training data</th><th>Mean predicted churn</th><th>Implied churners</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>39K sample</td><td>~50%</td><td>40.60%</td><td>12,180</td></tr>
          <tr><td>1M dataset</td><td>~2%</td><td>2.38%</td><td>713</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Retrained, the same architecture returned a test AUC of <strong>0.794</strong> — statistically
    indistinguishable from the 0.793 I started with. The ranking never changed. The number attached to
    each customer changed by a factor of seventeen.</p>

    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>AUC only asks whether riskier customers score higher than safer ones. It is unchanged by any
      transformation that preserves order — so a model can be <em>perfectly</em> ranked and
      <em>arbitrarily</em> mis-scaled, and no ranking metric will ever tell you. Lifetime value
      calculations use the level, not the order. Had I shipped the first model, every budget
      downstream would have been inflated seventeenfold.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Testing five retention programs</h2>
    <p>With probabilities on the right scale, I simulated five interventions by editing the input that
    each program targets — set overage charges to zero, set retention calls to zero — and re-scoring
    through the model.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Observed churn versus predicted churn after intervention</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">Each pair is one program, on the customers who would receive it. Hover
        any row for detail.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="article-seg" role="group" aria-label="Highlight">
        <button id="b-all" aria-pressed="true">All five</button>
        <button id="b-kept" aria-pressed="false">Funded only</button>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-legend">
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw article-sw-r" style="background:var(--s-a)"></span>Observed churn in group</div>
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw article-sw-r" style="background:var(--s-b)"></span>Predicted after intervention</div>
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw" style="background:var(--muted);height:2px;width:16px;border-radius:0"></span>Sample mean prediction, 2.38%</div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-chart-scroll"><svg id="chart2" viewBox="0 0 720 330" role="img"
        aria-label="Dumbbell chart of observed versus post-intervention predicted churn for five retention programs"></svg></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tip2"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
      <table class="article-table">
        <thead><tr><th>Program</th><th>Targeted</th><th>Observed churn</th><th>Predicted after</th><th>Funded</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody id="tbody2"></tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Read at face value, two programs made things worse — customer care and early-tenure engagement
    both showed higher churn after the simulated fix. The notebook I wrote at the time put this down
    to "how XGBoost combines things" and dropped them.</p>

    <div class="article-flagbox">
      <p><strong>That conclusion doesn't hold, and the error is mine.</strong> The two numbers in each
      pair aren't comparable. <em>Observed churn</em> is what actually happened to those customers.
      <em>Predicted after</em> is what the model says post-intervention. To isolate an intervention
      effect you have to compare the model's prediction <em>before</em> against its prediction
      <em>after</em> — same model, same customers, one variable changed. I never computed the
      before.</p>
      <p>New Handset Support proves the point. Its 26 customers contain zero actual churners, so
      observed churn is 0.0% — and against zero, any positive prediction looks like the program
      causes churn. That isn't an intervention effect. It's a 26-person sample with no events in it.</p>
    </div>

    <p>So the honest statement is not "two programs backfired." It is that <strong>the sign of the
    effect is unknown for four of the five</strong>, because the baseline was never measured. Only
    Usage-Based Plan is safe, and only because its gap is wide enough to survive the confusion.</p>
    <p>There's a second inconsistency I found on re-reading: First Call Resolution shows the largest
    apparent improvement of any service program — 3.32% down to 2.38% — and it was dropped from the
    economics anyway, while New Handset Support, which looks worse on the same flawed comparison, was
    kept. Neither decision follows from the numbers.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The economics that survived</h2>
    <p>For the programs that went forward, I valued each over a 60-month window, discounting at 10% a
    year. Breakeven is the most you could spend per customer before the retained revenue stops
    covering it; I proposed half that, as a margin against the effect being smaller than modeled.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
    <table class="article-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Program</th><th>Targeted</th><th>Breakeven / customer</th><th>Proposed / customer</th><th>Total budget</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Usage-Based Plan</td><td>16,264</td><td>S$407.80</td><td>S$203.90</td><td>S$3,316,229</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Student Bundle</td><td>1,654</td><td>S$452.36</td><td>S$226.18</td><td>S$374,101</td></tr>
        <tr class="dim"><td>New Handset Support</td><td>26</td><td>S$0</td><td>S$0</td><td>S$0</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      <tfoot><tr><td>Proposed total</td><td>17,944</td><td></td><td></td><td>S$3,690,330</td></tr></tfoot>
    </table>
  </div>
  <p class="article-fine">Figures in Singapore dollars. "Total budget" is proposed spend per customer × customers
  targeted — an investment ceiling, not a profit forecast.</p>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>One caveat belongs in the open rather than a footnote: the Student Bundle's S$452 breakeven does
    not come from the model at all. Occupation is categorical, so I couldn't simulate it the way I
    simulated overage. The 1.5% churn reduction behind that number is an <strong>assumption I
    chose</strong>. It happens to produce the highest breakeven in the table, which is exactly the
    situation where an assumption deserves to be labelled loudly.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The technical layer</h2>
    <div class="article-tech-label">For readers who want the mechanics</div>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Why oversampling breaks probabilities but not rankings</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>With ~2% churn, a 39,000-row sample holds only about 800 churners. Oversampling to 50/50 gives
    the model far more signal per unit of compute, which is why it's standard practice for rare events.</p>
    <p>What it changes is the intercept. The model learns P(churn | features) under a prior of 0.5 and
    reports that, even though the deployment prior is 0.02. Because the distortion is monotone, every
    rank-based diagnostic — AUC, gains, lift — is untouched. Every level-based use — expected churners,
    lifetime value, budgets — is wrong by roughly the ratio of the two priors.</p>
    <p>Two fixes exist. Re-estimate on data carrying the true base rate, which is what I did. Or keep
    the oversampled fit and correct the intercept analytically. Worth noting: the weighted logistic
    regression came out correctly scaled at 2.29% on the same sample, because the weights restored the
    prior. The tree ensemble had no such correction, and I didn't add one.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What "simulating an intervention" actually assumes</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Setting <code>overage = 0</code> and re-scoring is a convenient move that smuggles in two strong
    assumptions.</p>
    <p><strong>First, that the program works perfectly.</strong> Moving someone to a better-fitting plan
    is modeled as overage vanishing entirely, not shrinking. Real programs have partial take-up and
    partial effect.</p>
    <p><strong>Second, and more seriously, that the association is causal.</strong> XGBoost learned that
    customers with overage churn more. It cannot distinguish "overage charges cause people to leave"
    from "the kind of customer who overruns their plan is also the kind who leaves." Zeroing the
    variable answers a question about the <em>model</em>, not about the world.</p>
    <p>This is why the case asks for a randomized trial design alongside the simulation, and why my
    proposal was to split the target group 50/50 and measure churn at 30 days and at 3–6 months. The
    model estimate is a prior for sizing the pilot — not a substitute for it.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>How lifetime value was computed</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>For each targeted customer I projected monthly margin over 60 months, with survival to each month
    driven by the predicted churn probability, discounted at 10% annually. Running it twice — once at
    baseline churn, once at post-intervention churn — gives two lifetime values, and the difference is
    the value the program creates.</p>
    <p>Breakeven per customer is that difference. Spend exactly it and you are indifferent; spend less
    and you profit. The proposed figure is 50% of breakeven, which is a judgment call rather than a
    derived quantity, chosen because the effect estimates carry the uncertainty described above.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What I'd do differently</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p><strong>Compute the baseline prediction per group.</strong> This is the one real defect in the
    analysis. One extra line — the mean of the baseline prediction restricted to each target group —
    turns five ambiguous comparisons into five valid ones, and would likely change which programs got
    funded.</p>
    <p><strong>Check calibration deliberately, not accidentally.</strong> I caught the 17× error because
    the mean prediction looked implausible. That is luck, not method. A calibration plot alongside every
    AUC would have surfaced it immediately, and I now treat "what is the mean predicted probability, and
    does it match the base rate?" as a required check before any model touches money.</p>
    <p><strong>Drop the 26-customer program.</strong> New Handset Support cannot support any conclusion
    at that sample size. Reporting it as a S$0 breakeven implies a finding of "no value," when the honest
    statement is "no evidence either way."</p>
    <p><strong>Put a range on the lifetime values.</strong> A 60-month projection compounds the churn
    estimate sixty times. Small errors in the probability become large errors in the total, and a single
    point estimate hides that entirely.</p>
    </div>
    </details>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What this case taught me</h2>
    <p>Two lessons, and the second one only arrived on a second reading.</p>
    <p><strong>A model has two separate jobs, and passing one says nothing about the other.</strong>
    Ranking answers "who is riskiest?" Calibration answers "how likely is this, really?" AUC only audits
    the first. Any decision that multiplies a probability by money depends entirely on the second.</p>
    <p><strong>A comparison is a claim, and it needs the same scrutiny as a model.</strong> I built a
    careful model, corrected a serious scaling error, and then evaluated five programs against a baseline
    that couldn't support the conclusion I drew from it. The modeling was the easy part. Deciding what
    two numbers mean when you put them side by side is where the actual reasoning lives.</p>
    <div class="chips article-chips">
      <span class="chip">Churn modeling</span>
      <span class="chip">Probability calibration</span>
      <span class="chip">Class imbalance / oversampling</span>
      <span class="chip">XGBoost tuning</span>
      <span class="chip">CLV modeling</span>
      <span class="chip">Intervention simulation</span>
      <span class="chip">Experiment design</span>
      <span class="chip">polars</span>
    </div>
    <p class="article-fine">Figures are from my own analysis on the course dataset. The underlying case materials
    and data are proprietary to the publisher and are not reproduced here.</p>
  </section>
</div>

        hit.addEventListener("mouseenter",function(){
          g.classList.add("on");
          tip.innerHTML="<b>"+r.k+"</b><br><span class='article-tip-num'>"+r.n.toLocaleString("en-US")+
            "</span> customers<br>observed <span class='article-tip-num'>"+r.o.toFixed(2)+
            "%</span> → predicted <span class='article-tip-num'>"+r.p.toFixed(2)+"%</span><br>"+r.note;
          tip.style.opacity=1;place(tip,host,hit);
        });
        hit.addEventListener("mouseleave",function(){g.classList.remove("on");tip.style.opacity=0;});
        g.appendChild(hit);
        svg.appendChild(g);
        groups.push({g:g,r:r});
      });
      var xt=el("text",{x:ML,y:MT-14,"class":"article-ax"});
      xt.textContent="Churn rate";svg.appendChild(xt);

      tb.innerHTML=D.map(function(r){
        return "<tr"+(r.fund?"":" class='dim'")+"><td>"+r.k+"</td><td>"+r.n.toLocaleString("en-US")+
          "</td><td>"+r.o.toFixed(2)+"%</td><td>"+r.p.toFixed(2)+"%</td><td>"+
          (r.fund?"Yes":"No")+"</td></tr>";
      }).join("");

      function setMode(kept){
        document.getElementById("b-all").setAttribute("aria-pressed",!kept);
        document.getElementById("b-kept").setAttribute("aria-pressed",kept);
        groups.forEach(function(o){
          o.g.style.opacity = (!kept || o.r.fund) ? "" : ".28";
        });
      }
      document.getElementById("b-all").addEventListener("click",function(){setMode(false);});
      document.getElementById("b-kept").addEventListener("click",function(){setMode(true);});
    })();
  })();
</script>
